title: 4 months building my roguelite FPS with an AI pair programmer — what it's actually good at in UE5, and where it still lies to me
author: Snoo-29395
selftext:
NULLGATE is a PS1-style FPS roguelite I'm building alone in Unreal Engine 5 — procedural arenas, bullet-hell enemies, over 800 commits in 4 months. I couldn't have hit that pace solo without AI, so instead of just dropping the trailer out of context, I want to talk about what the workflow actually looks like, because it's not what I expected going in.

The biggest win wasn't code generation, it was code *conversation*. My arena generator builds levels as floating islands, decks with intentional holes, gaps between platforms, a whole city below, etc.

The place it consistently lies to me is UE5 specifics. it'll confidently invent engine API that doesn't exist, or give me a pattern that was true two engine versions ago. It struggle to use good practices. Coming from regular web development that was weird to me, so i look how to approach the task i want to do and feed that to the AI to create a good plan first.

One deliberate line I drew: zero AI art. Every asset is from free packs (Quaternius, KayKit and friends) unified by a shader I wrote — 312px render height, vertex snapping, animation stepped every 6th frame. Twenty different packs come out looking like one 1998 CD. I wanted the aesthetic to be a *decision*, not a generation, and honestly the shader does more for cohesion than any amount of bespoke art could at my budget (which is $0).

The Steam page just went live, wishlists are life or death for an unknown solo game, so if any of this sounds interesting:  
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5042810/NullGate/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=aigamedev](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5042810/NullGate/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=aigamedev)

Curious what others here have found: has anyone solved the "AI can't playtest" gap? Getting useful design feedback out of a model on something as feel-dependent as a shooter? And for the UE5 people, what do you find most hard to solve using AI rather than manual input?

replies.author: Snoo-29395
replies.body: Fable 5 until I get out of weekly usage and then opus 5, but I’ve been hating opus lately to be honest

replies.author: paulordbm
replies.body: It's been working really well for me but it does require a lot of work on the harness until you're happy with the output. I keep tweaking the project rules for everything, even communication, and I like to use skills a lot too but I'm still finding what works best for this kind of development. I use SDD with the Superpowers plugin for Cursor on my daily work and it's flawless but for game development this method feels too restrictive and bad for prototyping. But I'm getting somewhere. Do you have any recommendations for skills? I found a website once with loads of game-dev centric skills to download for free but haven't tried them. There seemed to be a few related to UE5's best practices.

replies.author: Snoo-29395
replies.body:
I'm kind of afraid of using skills to be honest, i analyze every one myself and then i also make the AI do it, in several occasions i found out that some of them tries to skip previous instructions and do malicious actions, but maybe i'm too paranoid honestly.

My process is:  
  
\- I set the official mcp skills md created by the unreal team, if you look at unreal engine github you will find it (not sharing any links just in case, no idea if it's allowed)

\- On every new task i basically investigate and try stuff until i found the best way of approaching the problem, once i found it (with a lot of back and forward), and i'm confident enough the approach is correct is save it into my skills.

\- No matter how small the task is, i always create a plan first and then implement, this way i can not only learn while doing, but also making sure the AI is going the correct path.

\- This one helped me A LOT: i have all my c++ code full of console logs. I'm avoiding blueprints whenever is possible, and even on blueprints i have console logs every now and then. This way, when i test the game in the PIE and something goes wrong, is way easier to track the bug, as the AI is virtually "seeing" my play through and can track the problem when something doesn't work.

  
\- I don't know if this is common in gamedev or is just me, but the context window reach 100% incredibly fast, so i try to compact sessions a lot. On top of that, i have a safeguard to know when the chat starts hallucinating. Is just a dumb rule saying that each message should start by calling me by my name. When i see Claude stops doing that, i know is time to start a fresh session.

\- One thing i couldn't tackle yet, and i think this is basically because AI is just bad at it, is level generation. I ended up generating a really good procedural map gen algorithm but it works because my lvls are PS1-style arenas, so not that many props or worldbuilding is needed, my main hub was placed manually for example. The best way i found to use the MCP to generate the barebones of a lvl, was to first ask the AI to create a sort of autocad diagram using claude design, and then translating that into a level. It works better when it has numers like height, width, position in space, etc.

  
I know all this are too general concepts but hopes it helps you in any way

replies.author: Snoo-29395
replies.body: One more thing. Before starting any plan, i ask it (it's a skill at this point), to search on the internet how other devs solved a similar problem and if there is a common practice on the genre, and i compare its findings with what i know

replies.author: paulordbm
replies.body:
You're basically doing everything I'm doing too. I also worked a lot on trying to give the agent more visibility of what's happening in the game. So for my game, specifically, we built tools that allow the agent to dump game state at any given time. And a replay system that stores player input and some initial state, then replay the inputs and re-simulates the game. This allows the AI to observe select game state for every single tick on that clip. So all of the clocks in my game are controlled by the code, we don't use engine clocks. My custom physics run at 240Hz, the presentation runs under a 60Hz clock my sim controls and feeds Unreal's animations, particles, etc. So of course there are some systems that can't be replayed with exact fidelity because they're not fully controlled by my core sim or they're not deterministic enough, but the important parts of the game, for now, are. This helps A TON for my case.

Apart from the official Unreal MCP skills, the only ones I'm using are Superpowers brainstorming, speccing, planning and plan-executing skills, and an academic-research skill I found on [skills.sh](http://skills.sh) that helps me a ton, similarly to what you mentioned about having the AI investigate how the industry does things. I have it search documentation, forums, blogs, presentations and scientific articles before making some architectural decisions.

One thing you didn't mention that I AM doing is having Fable work as a design or tech lead, orchestrating other subagents running Sonnet 5 or Opus 5 to perform the tasks. Fable designs, architects, dispatches, reviews, QAs, dispatches fixes, approves/rejects work, then report to me.

So I think we're in very similar boats tbh. This is all very new, everyone's learning from it all the time. An yes, the context is filled way too quickly when developing games. Not sure what it is but I think interacting with the editor via MCP or through the Python API seems to require a lot of tokens. Using subagents help a lot with that too because each subagent has their own context so it doesn't "pollute" the orchestrator's as much.

replies.author: Snoo-29395
replies.body: Thanks for the insight! I will absolutely try the replay system approach, sound much better than mine
